speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I ask the indulgence of the House to salute the 92 members of our armed forces to be honoured by the Governor General at Rideau Hall tonight. There they will participate in the investiture of the Order of Military Merit, a distinguished award for meritorious military service.
I understand that a number of the recipients are in the gallery today, and since only two of the 92 are of the fairer sex I am sure hon. members will not object to my naming Captain Edna Stokes, from the beautiful riding of Hamilton Mountain, for singular attention.

Hon. Allan ]. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council): Mr. Speaker, I thought it might be best to raise the point I am about to raise on motions. It has to do with certain discussions that have taken place about the length of speeches in the budget debate. I believe the whips have discussed a possible time limitation for each category of participants as follows. Party leaders would be limited to 40 minutes each and official spokesmen for parties and ministers would be limited to 30 minutes, but in either of these categories the time could be extended with the consent of the House. All other members would be limited to 15 minutes, without any opportunity to ask the House for additional time. The purpose really is to provide for the greatest possible participation in the debate. I thought I might make known to the House the purport of the discussions so that the proposal might be put in the form of a House order later if it is found to be agreeable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 to request the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on an issue of national urgency.
As automation plays a leading part in our economy, as an increasing number of Canadian citizens find themselves jobless without any possibility of finding work and without financial resources as soon as they reach the critical age of 55, and as this problem is getting more serious every day and no permanent solution seems to be applied at this time, I propose, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That this House instruct the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to make a thorough examination of the situation existing in the case of this group of people aged 55 and over, to analyse the possibilities of lowering old age security pensionable age to 60 and to report to this House.
February 21, 1973

STUDY OF EMERGENCY PROCEDURES BY LIEUTENANT-GENERAL DARE
speechtext:
1.	Has the study of emergency procedures conducted by Lieutenant-General Dare been completed and submitted for consideration?
2.	What are the terms of reference for the study?
3.	Is it the intention to continue the employment of the former Vice-Chief of the Defence Staff as (a) a public servant, on contract (b) an Order in Council appointment to the staff of the Privy Council or Prime Minister's Office?
4.	What will be the status of the conclusions of the Dare Study in relation to the Report by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, as tabled on June 29, 1972?
5.	Will the Standing Committee be given the opportunity of reviewing and commenting on General Dare's recommendations?
6.	Will General Dare's report be made public?
7.	Will portions of the report or summary of its findings be made public and, if so, which ones?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STUDY OF EMERGENCY PROCEDURES BY LIEUTENANT-GENERAL DARE
speechtext:
1. General Dare has submitted a summary of his major findings and conclusions and is now in the process of completing his report.
2.	On May 1, 1972, General Dare was given the following terms of reference:
In general to carry out the Cabinet decision of July 22, 1971, that "a study be initiated into the subject of crisis-handling methods and structures within the federal government with a view to determining the means whereby better control and co-ordination among departments and agencies in the handling of natural and man-made disasters can be effected."
To study and report on the problems of recognizing and defining "crisis-indicators" and of criteria which must be applied for any event and/or a trend to require crisis management action.
To study and report on crisis-sensing techniques and methods and techniques of crisis decision-making.
To study and report on the current state of crisis-management preparedness including such problems as control, co-ordination, communications, facilities and ministerial responsibilities and authorities.

Order Paper Questions
To study and report on the criteria which must apply in any crisis situation before the Prime Minister and the Cabinet would be required to exercise and perform emergency powers.
To study and report on such physical, organizational and procedural preparations as may be required to enable the Prime Minister and the Cabinet to exercise and perform emergency powers when a natural or man-made crisis occurs.
That for the purpose of this study LGEN Dare will be seconded to the Privy Council Office effective May 1, 1972, with necessary office space and equipment to be provided by the Privy Council Office and with a combination of loaned and seconded staff, providing that in the case of seconded staff the approval of the Director of Administration, PCO, will be required.
3.	Lieutenant-General Dare was seconded to the Privy Council Office from the Department of National Defence for the purpose indicated above. It is not intended to continue his employment there or in the Prime Minister's Office.
4.	In view of the terms of reference described above, it is expected that the conclusions of the Dare report will deal peripherally with some of the matters embodied in the Report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. By virtue of the terms of reference, the Dare study will have examined a much broader area. Until such time as the report has been studied it is not possible to say what the status of its conclusions will be in relation to the Standing Committee's report of June 29, 1972.
5.	This is a matter that will be considered after the government has had an opportunity to consider the report itself.
6.	It is the intention of the government to make the report public in due course. It is possible that some parts of it could raise security considerations which would have to be examined, but it seems likely that virtually all of the report can be released. Until such time as the report has been considered by the government, public disclosure will not be made.
7.	Yes. A full summary of findings will be made public in due course.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
speechtext: The Consumer Price Index measures the percentage change through time in the cost of purchasing a constant quantity and combination of goods and services. Starting with 1961, the index is based on 1957 family expenditure patterns while for the years 1949 to 1960 the index is based on 1947-48 expenditure patterns. The differing weight base periods are arithmetically linked to the time base 1961 = 100. In 1949, the Consumer Price Index averaged 77.4 and in 1972 it averaged 139.8. Is it the intention of the government to institute or extend coastal trading regulations, similar to the Jones Act in the United States, to include the east and west coasts of Canada and, if so, will they be extended to include all the Arctic sector and Arctic Islands?

The government is presently considering a new policy for the Canadian coasting trade largely on the basis of the Darling Report. This Report recommended reserving all coasting trade activities in Canada to Canadian-flag vessels and extending the laws to the Arctic waters and Continental Shelf of Canada. It was, however, the recommendation of Mr. Darling that where no Canadian vessel was available or adequate to fulfil the requirements of the trade permits would be granted to foreign vessels following payment of duties on the basis of the value of the ship and its period of activity in the coasting trade. The Jones Act in the United States does not allow foreign vessels to engage in the coasting trade. Perhaps it might be noted that the United States has virtually no coasting activity.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will be in a somewhat different mood this afternoon from the mood it was in the other night. Having spent some time profitably reading previous speeches of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on budgetary matters, I thought I might refer to those other speeches which he made from time to time. I have before me the speech the minister made last fall in Truro. Does he want to read it? In that speech, he referred to certain budgetary and fiscal measures proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). It occurs to me he would now want to swallow that speech after chewing it into small pieces- dry. That is the type of punishment he deserves for having made those statements.
I shall not plagiarize the delightful writings of other people who have compared passages in the various statements made by the minister at different times. One such statement was to the effect that the Leader of the Opposition had taken leave of his senses, that his fiscal proposals would increase the budgetary deficit to about $900 million, double what the minister had proposed in June; that it would drive the country to the edge of bankruptcy; that all those measures were utterly irresponsible and ill thought out. But what did the minister have to say the other night? "I come, now, to a budgetary proposal of the greatest significance", he told us. And then he laid out his personal income indexing proposal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you read George Bain's column?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All right. That's fine. I will go on to something else. I did refer to the opportunity I had had of reading some delightful writing. But not everybody has a chance of reading that column. I think people all over the country who read Hansard should
February 21, 1973

have the benefit of these comments. This applies also to the minister's speeches in Calgary. I do not know whether an increase from $1.5 billion to $2 billion would ever drive the country to bankruptcy. Yet why would the minister now come along and boast that for the good of the country we should now, in a deficit position, spend some $2 billion more? In June of last year he said such additional expenditure would drive the country into bankruptcy-it was sheer fiscal lunacy on the part of the Leader of the Opposition even to suggest we spend that kind of money. Yet now the expenditure of that amount is supposed to bring the biggest possible benefit to the country and constitute the greatest possible gesture on the part of the Minister of Finance. The hon. gentleman reminds me of the little fellow who pulled out a plum. He has been sitting in the corner and he has pulled out a plum. It is great to hear the minister, having said these things, now telling us that what was irresponsible, what was unacceptable, how they now become policy with the greatest possible benefit. Somebody has called this a chocolate bar budget. Perhaps others would call it a candy budget, recalling the Prime Minister's statement about all the candy which would be handed out-les bonbons que nous allons donner au public canadien.
Then I noticed that another eminent scribe had entitled his column this morning "Budget! Humbug!". Is that the kind of candy included in this budget? We will see.
More seriously, Mr. Speaker, the House was in a very anticipatory mood the other night, and so was the public in the galleries. The stage was set for what I would suggest was one of the most dramatic budget nights we have seen in many years. As my colleague from Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) has said, was this going to be the opening of the wedding presents to see whether the trial marriage between the NDP and the Liberals was going to continue? Was the NDP bride going to find these wedding presents satisfactory? I do not know, but perhaps that accounted for some of the anticipation. Others, particularly those behind the minister who were supporting him, were looking for what they might call political goodies, for those things that would make for a good pre-election budget, no matter if those measures were devoid of any principle. We must remember that the thing is to win the next election, and with a nice cushion of swollen tax receipts the minister would be able to play the bountiful Santa Claus to the Canadian public.
The minister would not tell the Canadian public, of course, that he was merely returning to them money extracted from them by a tax schedule provided for by section 117 of the act which the government of Ontario as well as the members of this House, including the NDP, had told the government would grossly gouge the Canadian public and place in the federal coffers funds far in excess of the government's requirements. We now have an admission that the public was being gouged. The minister says with some pride-at least, he thinks it should be with some pride-that he is leaving with the taxpayers some $1.3 billion as a result of the Income tax changes that are proposed in the budget. As I have pointed out, according to the table of revenue that appeared at page 26 of the minister's budget speech, there will be an excess this year
The Budget-Hon. Marcel Lambert
of $925 million over last year on the personal income tax account. This represents a growth in the Income tax collections of $2.2 billion. Talk about the government benefiting from inflation!
This is all part of the colouring of the atmosphere in this House the other night. However, there were legions all across this country who were looking to see whether the budget would propose some bold measures, measures that would be new departures to deal with the problems that have been with us for years. These problems have not been swept under a rug. The minister's predecessor used to say, having looked at one month's statistics, that the curve had levelled off and that therefore he could promise that we were going to do a lot better. I quoted that speech the minister made last May in which he solemnly declared that the cost of living index would be much improved during 1972, that we would do a great deal better in the field of unemployment. But what do we have? We have a level of increase in the cost of living now that is totally unacceptable to the Canadian people and it just cannot continue.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It matters not what it is that influences these cumulative increases. The government had the best of all possible surveillance of these matters, but it strikes me that the surveillance was from the tail of the ostrich with its head in the sand. In other words, they could do nothing, did not want to do anything, and they did nothing.
The personal income tax cut included in this budget is, of course, welcome; there is no doubt about that. But it is less than the figure proposed by the Leader of the Opposition during the last campaign, indeed less than that which we have been proposing all along. Certainly, it is less than what it should be today. It is satisfactory as far as it goes, and I will not gainsay anyone who is able to benefit from this tax reduction. But it only shows, as I have pointed out before, that the tax rates in 1972 grossly overcharged the Canadian public. We are now going to get a decrease in the schedule by one point per tax bracket during 1973. This step was taken by the minister's predecessor to, shall I say, alleviate the possibility of excessive taxation and is statutory.
I also accept the increase of $100 in the personal exemption, but I should point out that the 5 per cent increase in the cost of living has already eroded $75 of the exemption in one year. If you take 5 per cent of $1,500 you will get $75, which brings the $1,500 down, in effect, to $1,425. This $100 increase will make up for the erosion of last year and will provide a partial bridge for this year until the personal income index comes into effect in 1974.
One would have expected there would be some really bold measures to deal with the increase in the cost of living. After all, the minister is relatively new to the job and is not tainted by the attitude that had prevailed when his predecessor was minister. However, the thinking seems to be the same; this budget is set in the same mould as last year's. As I have pointed out, even a lot of the phrases are the same.
As far as the customs tariff reductions are concerned, we have had that sort of thing before, when the only

February 21, 1973
The Budget-Hon. Marcel Lambert
people who suffered as a result were Canadians. We all remember the acceleration of the Kennedy round cuts. There was no diminution in the cost of living index as a result of that move, and here we have a unilateral reduction in the customs tariff. Some of my colleagues in the field of agriculture, and others in the field of industry, tell me they cannot understand the philosophy of the government in making this unilateral move on the eve of new multilateral talks on the reduction of tariffs. Here, we have a whole series of bargaining points that have been given away.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are temporary reductions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Temporary?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right, for one year. I said so right in my speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These will not be temporary. I do not anticipate the minister having the opportunity of announcing in the House that he is revising these tariffs and increasing them again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not get over-anxious, Marcel.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister tells me not to get over-anxious about this but I am not the one to be over-anxious.
I sometimes wonder about some of the underlying philosophy of this budget. Knowing the minister's position in the hierarchy of the Liberal party, one wonders just what circumstances might have coloured this budget. I do not want to be personal about this matter, but I could suggest all sorts of possibilities.
Quite frankly, this budget has no real economic purpose and no central theme. For instance, does the minister wish to expand the economy and, if so, how will this budget affect regional economic disparities? Has the minister taken steps in this budget with regard to regional economic disparities?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the minister doing anything in respect of solving agricultural problems?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suggest that instead he is creating them in the horticulture industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't be silly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is so. Does this budget do anything for the building industry?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What part of the economy of Canada does the minister intend to benefit by this budget?
[Mi'. Lambert (Edmonton West).]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Canadian consumer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister says "the Canadian consumer". If that is so, why is there not one measure calculated to control the accelerating cost of living?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a policy of drift. This is a budget of tinsel, garland and candy. It is superficially attractive and lends itself to the kind of headlines I have seen to the effect that taxes are down and pensions are up. There are a number of proposals which we accept, and it would be quite wrong to reject them. Certainly, the minister will agree that the economic crunch of his budget must be related to the over-all impact. He has stated time and time again that he would attempt to deal with the problems of unemployment and inflation, but nowhere in this budget has he really attempted to do so. He has only expressed some fond hopes. The minister has become expert in professing fond hopes that the economy will somehow be cranked up, that we will see a flattening out of upward pressure on the CPI and also the creation of 330,000 jobs this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Last year it was 330,000, but this year it is 300,000.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was quite clear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is 300,000 this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't let your leader upset you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the minister believe that the sales tax reductions and the customs tariff reductions will really have an effect on food prices? These reductions certainly will not have an effect on the demand for and the price of houses.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about housing starts?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure we would all love to hear another factual speech by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). One of these days he will be good enough to bring his attention to bear on some of the true facts of this budget, and tell the Canadian people just how the cost of living is to be reduced and how employment will be increased. That hon. member passes through the city of Toronto regularly. Perhaps, he will tell us how this budget will in any way reduce the rapidly increasing cost of housing in that city. I should think he would have that matter very close to his heart, and we will anticipate his participation in this debate at some time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about right now?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He gives the government hell and then votes with them,.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In so far as the income tax cuts are concerned, they are generally acceptable to us. I spoke about the basic exemption for a married
February 21, 1973

couple. Perhaps this will take care of the erosion caused by inflation during 1972. However, there is one thing I should like to find out in respect of the minister's charge that the Leader of the Opposition's constant dollar proposal was an impossible one. Were the adjustments made with the consent of the provinces? Has the minister been able to get provincial consent? I hope he will tell me that. Will the individual tax return in 1974 provide for an application of the adjustment formula to only federal tax or will it also apply to provincial tax? Having made the proposal at this time, I hope the minister or one of his colleagues will be able to tell us that this has been negotiated with the provinces, or has been presented as a fait accompli on a take it or leave it basis. Will this only apply to the federal portion of personal income tax? The answer no doubt will be interesting.
The increases in old age security to $100 is a good step forward. It provides some $13 more than would have been provided on April 1 as a result of the cost of living factor which would come into play at that time. We would then have had basic old age security at $86 and some cents. The adjustments in respect of the guaranteed income supplement are in keeping with the adjustments to the war veterans allowances.
However, there is one thing I wish in respect of these adjustments, and that is that the minister had been in consultation with some provincial authorities in respect of those senior citizens who live in nursing homes or senior citizens' homes. I hope that those who are being maintained at public expense will not have the biggest part of this increase in old age security taken from them under the guise of increased rents. I hope the minister will be able to use his good offices in conjunction with those of provincial ministers from one end of the country to the other to see that this does not happen.
I am not trying to make sheep or goats of any of the provinces, ministers or municipalities in this regard, and I know that it may be the municipalities that are involved, but this is my sincere hope. I know that in many instances these homes face municipal tax increases. This could be a frustrating step. If we must have a deficit in one area it is the Canadian taxpayer who must accept the deficit, and let us not try to say it is being passed on to someone else. It is the Canadian taxpayer who ultimately bears the cost of any deficit, if there must be one, to look after senior citizens and those people in public institutions who are better off there than they would be on their own.
There is some relief in respect of customs duties on such things as bagatelle tables, billiard tables, squash rackets, cricket bats and things of that sort. There is also some relief in respect of certain types of vegetables and fruits, and I am sure some of my colleagues from areas in British Columbia and the Niagara Peninsula will have more to say about this. There are others who will have something to say with regard to white hardware. I am not satisfied that this will prove to be a particularly good move. I am not satisfied this reduction will be passed on in any way to the consumer. Is there to be a monitoring system? We have had expressions of pious hopes in the past in respect of the reduction or removal of sales taxes so that the benefit could be passed on to the consumer if the purpose of the reduction is to fight the cost of living.
The Budget-Hon. Marcel Lambert

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you see what Eaton's said today?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but next month it may be nothing. I know what the Hudson's Bay Company and others have done. I know what the chocolate bar people have said. Some of them have said they will just make a bigger bar for 15 cents.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A bigger buy for your money.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For more money. I know it would have cost the public treasury $200 million or $250 million more, but the minister could have done much more good in the battle against the inflating cost of living by taking off the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. That step would be directly identifiable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is to be
monitoring.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In respect of the sales tax reductions on children's clothing, has the minister a system of monitoring to see that this will be of benefit? May I ask the minister how much of that reduction or elimination of sales tax would be absorbed by the counter effect of the 10 per cent devaluation of the Canadian dollar. Childrens clothing which is imported from Japan would cost probably 16 per cent more than the present level. Goods from Hong Kong would cost from 8 per cent to 10 per cent more.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely, you are not blaming me for what the Janapese are doing?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that the minister should not tell us in his speech that the reduction in sales tax on children's clothing and on these other commodities will have a very marked effect on the extent of the increase in the cost of living. The minister would have had to take 50 per cent, if he had that much tax on, in order to counterbalance the increase due to devaluation. The point is that building materials come mostly from Canada and the United States where there is not this difference as a result of the change in monetary valuation. I would suggest also to the minister that it is much easier to monitor, as a result of the concentration of these materials, the removal of the 11 per cent or 12 per cent tax from various categories of building materials. I believe the minister would have been further ahead had he spent another $250 million in this area because I suggest that his budget is not expansionary enough.
If one looks at the tables that were given to us yesterday by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) in so far as the spending estimates of the government are concerned, one will recall that that minister said there was a difference of some $2200 million in the estimates between 1972 and 1973. The main claim the minister makes is that he has an expansionary budget. Let us look at table one which appears at page 16. If one looks at the budgetary estimates and non-budgetary estimates for 1972-73 and compares them to 1973-74 one can see there is not a

February 21, 1973
The Budget-Hon. Marcel Lambert difference of $2200 million. There is less than $900 million that the President of the Treasury Board called principal estimates. He conveniently forgot the $1800 million which came in as a supplementary estimate which we just passed. It is the other estimates at which we must look. Therefore, there is no question that this is an expansionary budget. This blue book of estimates reports the spending program of the government.
Now, in respect of the 5 per cent cost of living increase factor let us see where one stands in relation to the 1972-73 estimates. That amount of $800 million I spoke about disappears. Therefore, outside of the inflationary factor, and applied to last year's estimates, there is no change and yet this is supposed to be an expansionary budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will end up with a big surplus again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister made certain proposals with regard to tax reform. It is unfortunate that many taxpayers will be caught in a real bind this year. I hoped the minister could have had a word to give these people, because the law of 1971 says that they had to take certain action by 1973. The action taken by the taxpayers was supposed to be subject to regulations, but the regulations have not even been drawn up. Is there no way that the minister could have indicated, for instance in respect of the foreign affiliates provisions of the Income Tax Act, that the date which appeared in Bill C-222 would be changed. There are taxpayers in this country who, if they are to follow the law, will have to undertake extensive administrative changes. However, nothing has been said.
A similar situation exists in respect of discretionary trusts where the beneficiaries are supposed to make elections according to certain regulations. Substantial assets of Canadians, not strangers, are involved in this and yet these regulations have not even been drafted let alone promulgated. The minister has given no indication in this regard. I would hope he would have his colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) stand in his place during this debate and make an authoritative statement in respect of all these matters. I know it will take some time to get Bill C-222 before this House and passed, but the taxpayer is entitled to justice. His fate should not be to be kept dangling in suspense because of the inability of the Finance Department, the Department of National Revenue or the other people involved in finance to agree or because of the deletoriousness at the cabinet level in agreeing on certain provisions. The taxpayer is entitled to a better deal than that.
There was one point that was raised by the Minister of Finance in answering the Leader of the Opposition, with regard to the $890 million which appears as a statutory item under the Department of Manpower and Immigration. This is a bookkeeping entry, but it is not part of an expansionary budget. It does not put one dollar into the economy. All it does is to meet the deficit in the unemployment insurance account which is finally computed with accuracy at the end of April. It goes to repay the advances the Minister of Finance has made under section 134 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is all that the $890

million does. It appears as part of this total $19 billion. As a matter of fact, I find that this year's estimates are below last year's, if one looks at the effect of the increasing cost of living which affects the government as much as it does anybody else. If the inflationary factor is applied, and this $890 million is not included, then this year's estimates are well below last year's. Not one dollar of this $890 million will ever appear in circulation; it is a bookkeeping entry.
This budget was supposed to deal with the problem of unemployment. Of course, it is an added bust when it comes to that. There is not within one ministry one proposal that actually makes a constructive effort to expand the economy. There is nothing there that will provide one meaningful job. There are some additional transfer payments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Long overdue.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will be transfer payments; they will increase pensions; they will pay more under medicare and for health care. But that does not increase the number of jobs for Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where are those jobs?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those are the things that we want to see. Having made these criticisms of the budget, and having indicated how the minister has failed to face up to the principal economic problems of this country, let me point out the third economic problem in this country, which looms large in the minds of many people, namely, the smaller degree of participation by Canadians in the ownership of Canadian business and development. The minister had a wonderful opportunity in this budget to do something positive with regard to that situation. There were many things he could have done to help Canadians acquire a bigger share of their own assets in business, and I do not care what kind of business it is, or a greater measure of control in their own resource development. I know that the minister's colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has a bill on the order paper, but the bill is entirely negative. It says: thou shalt not, thou shalt not, thou shalt not, all the way through. But does it tell Canadians: you may, or, you will be allowed to?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor does it say: we will help you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is the type of positive action that should be taken, and it could have been taken simply through amendments to the Income Tax Act. Why is there even a partial continuation of the principal occupation rule which bars Canadians from participating in resource development on equal terms with their American counterparts? You have tied the hands of Canadians behind their backs. You have done it for years. Certainly, in Bill C-259 there was a partial relief, but it was only partial; you untied one tiny knot but that arm is still up behind the back. In other sectors there are snack-les round the ankles of Canadians as taxpayers in competition with foreigners in the development and ownership of Canadian resources.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The administration moved in the right direction to eliminate estate taxes. The province of Alberta went the right way in not moving into that field. I trust that the province of Quebec will live up to its promise to do the same and that Ontario will do the same because in my book, in so far as the ownership and development of Canadian business and enterprise is concerned, there has been no greater shackle than the piracy under the succession duty legislation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have seen hundreds and thousands of Canadian businesses that have had to come on the market at fire sale prices in order to meet the rapacious demands of the government's financial policy, the pound of flesh of the "have-nots" and of those who have worked in this country. It is an outdated method going back to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in Britain to break up landed estates. It is of no application in this country. How many good Canadian businesses, from small ones to major ones, have had to go on the market, and who was there with the money to buy the shares at fire sale prices? There were our friends south of the border and our friends across the ocean. There is not one member in the House who cannot call to memory some classic examples of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have been blind. I can tell you of any number of them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your tears for the poor millionaires who are dying really shower over me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are not millionaires, Mr. Speaker, many of them. We want to pile on the agony higher and higher succession duties. They will find out who sells before succession duties come on and how they sell and to whom they sell.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you have an opportunity to buy some, what are you yelling about?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would have said that by changing the Income Tax Act, by persuasion with regard to succession duties, this situation could be avoided. Since the minister apparently had another good look at some of the fiscal proposals of the Leader of the Opposition and he found some to his liking, what about the small business investment tax credit that the Leader of the Opposition proposed to encourage Canadians? That would help Canadians to take a share in Canadian business.
I would like to make a proposal with regard to our resource development, and this would not cost the government anything at this time. Let us determine what is resource development from one end of the country to the other, and let us reserve this privilege for the average Canadian citizen and say to him: "Canadian, invest $1,000, $5,000". After all, what money can the average Canadian have? Invest it in the equities of whatever company or development you want within the ball park of the determined resource development. Then, you can sell that
The Budget-Hon. Marcel Lambert
stock and buy another as long as you keep your capital and accrual to your capital within that ball park. If you want to get out at the end of one year and there is a capital gain, we will forgive you 20 per cent and then 20 per cent for each succeeding year. For instance, if the Minister of National Revenue has left our good friend the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) with a few shekels and he has been able to invest $1,000 in resource development equities and finds at the end of five years they are worth $1,200, that is a $200 capital gain. One hundred dollars of that would be taxable, but because he has held the investment for five years we will forgive him the capital gains tax. This would apply to Canadian citizens only.
You may say that we are discriminating, but do we not all discriminate in some form or another? The government's legislation is certainly discriminatory when it comes to foreign takeovers and control of foreign investment. What-I am saying is that within the Income Tax Act there would be an advantage available to Canadian citizens only to invest in Canadian resource development. Unless the investment is made, there is no tax that is lost; a taxable income will be earned providing the investment is there but there must be an incentive.
This is not a novel plan, Mr. Speaker. A variation of it has been tried in other countries, such as Australia, where the degree of ownership of natural resource development is far higher than in Canada because of such an incentive. This is, I suggest, a positive gesture in favour of Canadians owning a greater share of the resource development of this country.
Coming to the point-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Coming to the point of unemployment and those massive measures needed to turn the corner, Mr. Speaker, all sorts of proposals have been tried by the government over the past several years but there were still 688,000 people seeking work this last month.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can we, as Canadians, in good conscience continue to say that we can carry this load, that this becomes something we must get accustomed to, that it is something we have to bear like arthritis or rheumatism? Of course not. I would have thought that the Minister of Finance would have seized the opportunity to do something bold and imaginative. I would say that he should not have been content with this set of estimates which frankly are no greater than last year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Throw it at him, Marcel.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He couldn't make it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Don't tempt me. On the
basis of his forecast as to the gross national product and income, the minister should have said "I am going to make a massive attack on unemployment with a real

expansionary budget. Something drastic has to be done; the corner has to be turned and we have not done it so tar."
My colleagues the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and my leader are going to elaborate on this point. On this occasion, a Conservative minister of finance would have introduced a really expansionary budget and if you want figures it could be $21 billion or $3 billion to really do a job and at the same time not be afraid to impose a total price freeze and then phased price controls in order to contain inflation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We saw the example of a price freeze and phased controls in the United States. There will be some argument as to how effective it was at the time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Food prices went up in the United States by 3 per cent in one month.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are you doing in Canada?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The point is this, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is this the point?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member who keeps yapping in the background would never understand in a year of Sundays. The minister should understand that the inflation psychology was blunted in the United States. The minister has another step to take as far as taxation is concerned and this is to turn that psychology-to get away from this anticipation of continuing inflation. The minister knows very well that there is a national psychological feeling with regard to inflation. Other countries have taken such steps and it would be in the interest of Canadians to do the same. The Conservative party would not be afraid to do this at this time. In future, if the circumstances are the same, I am satisfied that such steps would be taken without hesitation.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
To strike out all the words after "that" and substitute the following:
While acknowledging certain beneficial provisions in the budget proposals, this House regrets that they do not contain measures that will substantially reduce continuing high unemployment, effectively contain the spiralling cost of living or provide any incentives to Canadians to increase their participation in Canadian business enterprise and development.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in looking at this amendment I see that caution got the better of the drafters and they did not add the words "like the last Conservative government" when I think we had 10 per cent unemployment in this country. It is always a pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to follow the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert); of course, I mean to follow him in the sense of time rather than in the sense of agreeing with him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is because you have never understood it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In a few moments, as I listened to what he said, I thought he would support the budget. He seemed to suggest that there are all kinds of good things in it, things that he supports; yet, somehow or other, he never quite made that statement. I think he came down in favour of virtually everything except bringing back the enclosure laws.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You know, it is hard for a man to have faith anymore. It is hard to know what one can believe in.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Waterloo is the right constituency for the hon. member. He will soon meet his Waterloo.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At one time, the Conservative party was the party of fiscal integrity. You knew where it stood.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So did the Minister of Finance, and now look at him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: However, when the spokesman for the Conservative party says that the $2 billion deficit-and this is really something-is not sufficient, it is apparent that the day of balanced budgets is over and fiscal responsibility has gone by the board. We decided we were going to support this budget-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surprise, surprise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member means, support the trained seals on the government side.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see how responsive my friends in the official opposition are. I think I should make clear what we are supporting.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We know; your own political hides.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, yes. There is no surtax on them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are supporting specific measures contained in this budget, and not those contained in the previous budget brought down last May. This is a much better budget. I know the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has taken on himself the onerous task of being our conscience and advising us on how we should maintain our purity. I do not want him to think we do not appreciate him, because we do appreciate him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stanley is in shock.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let him get his facts straight so that, while acting as our conscience, he does not inadvertently become misled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stanley is still in shock.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me explain our position. This is not a budget that we, if we were a government, would have brought down. We have reservations about many provi-


sions in this budget. We have reservations about the size of the deficit. We think it should have been larger, that more stimulation should have been applied.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, yes. We had other considerations in mind. Perhaps the deficit will not be the determining factor in the amount of employment that will be created in this country. That is one of many considerations which must be taken into account. We suggest that there must be a change in the mix of economic policies followed in this country. We must move away from resource development that does not provide job opportunities and move into the manufacturing sector that does provide them. There is considerable evidence to indicate that, in the past, the size of deficits has not been the only important consideration.
I recall that in 1960-61 the Conservative government of the day, faced with a 10 per cent unemployment rate, also budgeted for a deficit but failed to create jobs. Why, Mr. Speaker? I will tell you why. When the government was budgeting for a deficit capital was coming in, resource development was taking place, interest rates was being forced up, our dollar was too high, and these factors tended to nullify any effects that might otherwise have been felt from the budget deficit. Unless the government introduces a whole range of policies designed to bring down the level of our dollar and curb resource development, and this c.an be done by accepting the Carter Commission proposals and taxing resource industries more heavily than now, the budgetary deficit in itself will not be sufficient.
The increase in old age pensions, although highly acceptable and welcome, is not one with which we are prepared to be satisfied. We will not be satisfied with the increase announced and will continue to urge the government to increase that amount again. I think this is the position my party has taken for a long time, and it is a position that the party will continue to take. It was not many years ago that J. S. Woodsworth stood in this House and pleaded for a $20 old age pension. We can look back on those years with satisfaction. We have not achieved everything we wanted, but we have certainly come some distance from those days. I think my colleagues and I can take great pleasure in knowing that, from time to time, we have been in the position of exerting influence on governments to increase the old age pension in accordance with precepts of equity and justice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have reservations about the indexed income system, that great idea the Liberals stole from the Conservatives. I know there is a poverty of ideas within that party, as well as on the government side. That, certainly, was not one of their better ideas. The indexed income issue was phony from day one, because if you adjust income tax rates from year to year you will achieve exactly the same results. Nevertheless, the government saw fit to steal that idea from the Conservative party. I understand the Conservatives are feeling uncomfortable. They are not accustomed to having their ideas stolen. After all, why steal from them? If you are going to steal, why go to an empty cupboard?
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are more accustomed to having our ideas stolen. Actually, in a sense, we wear clothes with large seams, to make sure that when they are stolen they are suitable for others. In time, the great Progressive Conservative party will become accustomed to the idea and accept it with the graciousness that one should acquire from this sincere form of flattery. I will return to the indexed tax system later. At this time, I merely want to note my reservations about it. I do not think it will do a great deal of harm or a great deal of good. I simply think it was a phony issue; nevertheless, there it is.
On balance, this is a better budget than any I have ever seen brought before this House-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -by any majority government. It is far from perfect, and we have reservations about it. If you compare this budget with the kinds of budgets Canadians have had to swallow from majority governments, I think you can say on balance that there has been an improvement. I am including Conservative as well as Liberal governments in my comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will not swallow it for more than six months, if you are here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know where the hon. member will be, but I intend to be here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought you were not going to run again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will be here until then. While we recognize that we did not get everything we wanted, the government accepted many ideas we have been putting forward for a long time. My party has 31 seats in this House and we took 18 per cent of the vote in Canada in the last election. We do not expect, because circumstances have placed us in the position of exerting enormous bargaining power, to use that power to extract everything we want.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think we have the right to do that. On the other hand, we have the responsibility to act on behalf of the voters who voted for us in this country and gave us the seats we hold. We have always held seats in this House and people have always voted for us but, because there have been majority governments, our influence was not given the recognition that it deserved. In a majority House, all parties have influence. That is the way it should be. This government has accommodated itself to us, and so it should have, not only this time but at all other times in the past. It is the failure of majority governments to accommodate minorities that should be condemned, rather than the failure of minority governments to accommodate minorities in this House.
Instead of the 3 per cent tax cut that the government would have been content with before the last election, there is to be a 12 per cent tax cut. Mr. Speaker, it is a 12
