The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
per cent tax cut and it is a progressive tax cut. The government has, in fact, accepted in an indirect way one of the proposals we have been making for a tax credit. The idea of having a lower minimum of $100 and a maximum of $500 is basically the same principle as a tax credit. It increases the progressiveness of the tax system to a remarkable degree. As my leader said, this is not the millennium, but it is the acceptance of an important principle that the chief beneficiaries of tax cuts should be at the lower rather than at the higher end of the taxation scale. To the extent that this is being accepted, we are for it. It is four times more than Canadians would have gotten under other circumstances.
The old age pension is being increased by roughly 15 per cent. Veterans pensions have been increased by roughly the same amount. Even the farmers have received some benefits this time. As I recall, in the last budget there was not a single word about farmers. It was as though they did not exist. It looks as though the government in its desperation to remain in office, and I am glad it got desperate enough to think about this, went back over our amendments and decided to pick up some of the ideas we advocated, and in fairness, some of the ideas the Conservatives and Social Credit party advocated.
I remember arguing strongly, as did other members from Saskatchewan, that a farm should be passed on to a son or another member of the family without the payment of a capital gains tax. At the time we moved that amendment, the obstacles for the Liberal party seemed insurmountable. Somehow or other, those obstacles have melted away. We are glad the idea has been accepted and, I think, it has been accepted in a very intelligent way. As long as the farm passes to a member of the family who continues to farm, no capital gains tax is payable. If the farm passes into speculation or some other use, a tax becomes payable, which is right and proper.
There has been a return to measures that permit the building of herds. This is an argument that was made by people in our party as well as the Conservative party. Under the previous tax system, the possibility of building a herd in the early years was not being treated with the consideration it deserved. The government has moved to correct that. To that extent, I think the present budget is useful.
The Minister of Finance, with all his taking ways, has apparently played no favourites. He has robbed everybody. Everyone has had to give up something, involuntarily of course. He is taking from everyone. The government is repaying an obligation it has owed the Social Credit party since 1963 when that party supported their motion and brought down the government. I note the son of the leader of the Social Credit party spoke with approval on the government's position to raise the old age pension and gave the Social Credit party the credit. That party had been advocating a $350 a month pension for married couples. He feels that the $330 is very much in line with what they wanted and he seems to be somewhat satisfied.
As I said earlier, the government also took an idea from the Conservatives, such as it was. I know this will reinforce the belief of the Conservative party that it pays to

advertise. All the running around this country advocating this idea, publicizing it, and speaking about it over television and to newspaper men has paid off. The Conservatives got what they wanted. The government accepted their idea. I presume that if they have an idea like that in the future, they will restrict it to the confines of their caucus in case the Minister of Finance steals it.
Something was taken from everyone. Even the page boys got to the receptive Minister of Finance on the candy bars. He has been very accommodating in that way. I would not want to have it appear that the Minister of Finance is a man totally devoid of ideas, because he is not. He has a lot of ideas, one of which is the leadership of the Liberal party. He has a lot of ideas aside from that. In fact, he has done some significant things in this budget and should be given credit for them.
One thing that was done, and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) did not think very much of this, was to unilaterally reduce the tariffs on certain items that do not significantly affect employment in Canada. That is an important step. I do not remember another occasion when a government unilaterally removed tariffs. If they did, I do not remember when it was. Whenever there was such a reduction in the past, it was always based on trading off something we have against something another country had. I realize this is only a temporary reduction and the trading potential is still there. It may be somewhat diminished. I hope the minister will not deny that. Nevertheless, the potential is still there.
What is important is that the government is prepared to use an instrument of policy to control consumer prices, something it should have used a long time ago. As long ago as the MacQuarrie commission report on combines, the recommendation to the government was that when you find collusion in the market place and working people are not affected by having some advantages passed along to the consumer, the government should act to remove their tariff protection. They have never done that. On each occasion where collusion was found and a recommendation for tariff removal should have been in order, the government took the position that it could not do it because it would be giving away its bargaining rights at the next round of negotiations. An insignificant fine was levied against the monopolies and they charged what the traffic would bear.
This particular measure, although it does not affect an enormous range of products, still affects enough products for it to have an impact. Its chief impact will not be that prices will be dramatically lowered as a result of the action that was taken. Its chief impact will be, if the government is alive to what it is doing, a warning to industries that do not pass on the savings they should that a government can make a recommendation to have their tariff protection removed. In the long run, it is important for this country to move toward tariff removal. Because of the nature of our country and the feeling in the west against tariff protection, the more we move in that direction without harming those industries which are in a special position, the better things will be. Therefore, I welcome that particular proposal in the budget. I see it as an innovative proposal for which the Minister of Finance should take some credit.
February 21, 1973

I said earlier that the inclusion of a minimum and a maximum amount for reduction of the income tax is a good feature because it increases the progressiveness of the tax schedule. I am glad to see that the government, after its conversations with the provincial governments, has moved to accept one of their arguments for including school taxes in the tax base. That is very important to many of the provinces.
Let me turn now, to another item in this budget which I feel to be of significance. I have said many nice things about the Minister of Finance. I think this particular thing was not by design. It is something he tripped over in his desire to keep support in this House. We have suffered enormously in this country from a decision made by Liberal governments of previous years that the worst thing we have to face in Canada is inflation rather than unemployment. As a result of that decision, this country was plunged into an unnecessary recession. There were enormous losses in production, untold hardship among the unemployed and enormous damage to our capacity as a nation to do good things and move ahead. It was a disastrous policy on the part of the Liberal government when they decided that inflation was the number one enemy. Inflation was, of course, an important matter. No one can dismiss it as insignificant.
But far more important was the need to concentrate on getting people to work, on providing jobs for Canadian people. Advice given at the time was ignored. Everything the government did was designed to contain an inflation which was largely international. This budget changes that pattern in a number of ways: first, by recognizing that it is necessary to run a sizeable deficit. I think most people will agree with me that the deficit was not large enough but it is a continuation of a deficit and it is bound to have an inflationary affect at the same time that it is stimulating the economy. But more than that, members opposite have accepted a principle we have put forward on many occasions. Yet, let us do what we can to contain inflation, but let us not kid ourselves that we can contain every aspect of inflation. Therefore, let us assure that those on fixed incomes are compensated while we are fighting the fight against inflation and not held, as they have been held, as hostages to a government with intentions that it could not match with action. Now, that has been accepted. The old age pension is indexed. You have gone beyond that. Veterans pensions are indexed and now they have picked up the Conservative idea of indexing the income tax.
As I said earlier, I do not think it is a very good idea, but it is an acceptance of a certain kind of principle. There is nothing much to get excited about one way or the other, because what is really important about the taxes people pay is the rate. It doesn't much matter whether you make this adjustment of 4 per cent up or down or in or out or sideways. That has been accepted. If you want to subtitle the minister's speech, it might be called "How to limit inflation and like it." It frees the minister's hands, now, to start moving this country ahead. These indexes are "in" and those who are going to be hurt by inflation will be compensated. Therefore, the government's No. 1 priority has to be the same as it should have been in the past, namely to get full employment in Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
In October, when the dust had cleared, parliament wound up in an unusual position. The early talk was that the country would be ungovernable and that parliament would be unmanageable. All of us were given a share of power. The question was, how would each party use that power. The Liberals have less power than before and they have proven themselves somewhat more accommodating as a result. Even the language in the House has improved to some extent. How have the Conservatives behaved?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Terribly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are right, they have behaved terribly. They have a little more power than they had before, and it has gone to their heads. All they can think of is bringing the government down and getting themselves in. If the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) were here, he could tell a story of how he laughed at the Liberals in 1957 when they suggested to him, get out, get out and let us in; we are the chosen. Now, the Conservatives seem to have picked up the same theme. They are the chosen and the Liberals should make way for them. I do not think it is a position which would be accepted in the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let's find out.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will find out soon enough. You certainly did not get any endorsation in the last election.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor did you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, we didn't get one, but we have not let it go to our heads, either!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Given such a situation, the responsibility of making parliament work has to a large extent fallen on the New Democratic Party. Some hon. members may laugh, but that is because they do not want parliament to work. We campaigned on the basis that we were going to make parliament work, and that is our commitment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is why, on a budget which has been designed to meet some of our objectives, and the objectives of other political parties, we think those responsible for it are deserving of support. It is for that reason we intend to support them. We intend to live up to our responsibility of seeing that parliament functions as long as it brings in good legislation. That should be clear. I should like to repeat what I said earlier. Our support is for this budget and for the ways and means motions which flow from this budget alone. There should be no misconstruing of the position of the New Democratic Party in relation to other matters which may come before us.
This budget has got something for everyone. Economists will like it because of the tariff proposals; consumers will like it for a similar reason; old age pensioners are receiving some benefits, veterans are receiving some benefits, farmers are receiving some benefits, small business is receiving some benefit; all taxpayers are receiving some benefits and the provinces are receiving some benefits. It has been without a doubt one of the most political

February 21, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Matte
budgets this country has ever seen and I say "political" in the best meaning of that word. Some of those great economic budgets which were designed by governments with a large majority turned out to be complete fiascos. This time, out of sheer necessity, out of the need to adapt itself to the various opinions held in this House, I think we have a political budget which is a good budget. Speaking to me about it the other day, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) called it a survival budget, a survival kit. Well, it is a survival kit. It is the government's survival kit. If I may quote Samuel Johnson:
Depend on it, Sir, when a man knows he is to be hanged in a fortnight it concentrates his mind wonderfully.
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the Minister of Finance on his powers of concentration?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were really eager to hear the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) last Monday.
I do not know whether the fact of having been chosen the fifth best-looking Canadian, male had some effect on him, but he seems to have rewarded his supporters with candy.
So many promises had been made! So nice things had been suggested! Such a renewed governmental policy in the economic and social fields had been predicted that we were expecting a budget repleted with social and economic measures meant to give satisfaction to Canadian taxpayers.
We had been told, Mr. Speaker, that the government had seen the light in October last when the Canadian electors had clearly indicated that they were not satisfied with its performance and had threatened to remove it, if it did not amend shortly.
The Liberal government had then promised to mend its ways, to make it up with the people and listen to their most urgent requests and it had then brought forward a Throne Speech which enabled us to believe that it was finally to govern in the best interests of the Canadian people.
Having heard Monday night the Minister of Finance make amends and admit the past mistakes and faults of the Liberal government, having heard him implicitly state that the government had failed to find employment for those who wished to work and that family budgets are burdened as a result of price increases and taxes of all kinds, we were expecting more thorough reforms, more effective measures to solve the unemployment problem in order to assure the security of all Canadians and reduce prices to an acceptable level for Canadian consumers.
Now, what does the Minister of Finance say in his budget? The purpose of this budget, he says, is to bring about a substantial reduction in unemployment. The budget, he adds, is aimed at the faster growth of our economy, at reducing inflationary pressures and the squeeze of rising prices on family budgets. Finally, this budget, according to the Minister of Finance, is aimed at increasing the real income and improving the standard of living of Canadians.
[Mr. Saltsman.l
That means, Mr. Speaker, that the minister recognizes the gravity of the unemployment situation. The government admits that our economy is not healthy. This means as well that they admit that inflation was not licked and this finally means that they admit that many Canadians are in need and deserve a better fate.
Mr. Speaker, has the Minister of Finance taken the necessary steps to prevent thousands of Canadians from being unemployed? Does that mean that the Minister of Finance announced the decision of the government to secure economic security for all Canadians? Finally, does that mean that the hon. Minister of Finance found a way to stop the inflation and the rapid increase in prices which continuously swallows up an ever increasing part of family budgets?
To find an answer to these questions, Mr. Speaker, we will analyse some of the proposals contained in the budget to find out if the announced measures will be enough to solve the present problems of our economy.
In the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday February 20, 1973, the editorial is entitled: "The Candy Budget". The author reminds us that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has undertaken, in a speech which will undoubtedly last for ever, that if the government was reelected, it would distribute goodies to the people of Canada. According to the Gazette, the hon. Minister of Finance took this statement seriously since he announced the removal of the sales tax on chocolate bars.
In its Tuesday issue, the Toronto Globe and Mail also speaks about "candy kisses" contained in the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance.
Finally, in the Journal de Montreal published on Tuesday, one can read the following title: "At last we have them, Trudeau's candies" and reporter Jacques Guay writes about it, and I quote:
Mr. Trudeau keeps his promises. He promised "candies", lots of candies to Quebecers. He kept his word in his first minority budget. If the manufacturers do not keep everything for themselves, we will pay less for Pepsi, chips, make-up, Dentyne gum and Caramilk bars, thanks to Mr. Turner's last budget.
That then is the tone the Minister of Finance gave his budget: "candies", cheaper candies, Dentyne gum, and soda-pop, more crumbs. But that budget does not hold anything of sustenance. Yet, they claim they want to solve the problem of unemployment and give economic security to the Canadians.
First, let us study the celebrated matter of the cuts in excise tax and duties on some imported goods. In his "Supplementary Information on the Budget", the Minister of Finance explained as follows:
The budget proposes important new exemptions from the federal sales tax and the removal of special excise taxes on many consumer items. While the changes are effective immediately, their full impact on retail prices may not be felt until goods upon which the taxes have already been paid move to retail shelves and are sold.
When he brought down his first budget on May 8, 1972, the minister stated that the economic expansion would put an end to unemployment and that inflation would at last be controlled.
February 21, 1973

We know what happened. The rate of unemployment has kept on going up while prices are at a record high. That should give us an indication of what we should believe when the Minister of Finance tells us that the cuts in sales taxes and excise taxes will benefit the Canadian consumer.
What gives to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) assurance that lowering the sales tax and removing special excise taxes will benefit the consumer and not the retailer? What gives him assurance that some retailers will not take the opportunity either to increase their profits or to try to improve their unsteady situation because they have difficulty in striking a balance and meeting their expenditures? Who then will benefit from these lower sales and excise taxes and what measures will the government take in order that these cuts are really passed on to the consumer?
And why have especially chosen chocolate bars or Den-tyne chewing gum as typical products on which the government wants to make sales taxes disappear?
For years now, Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit party of Canada and other opposition parties have been asking the government to eliminate that nuisance tax on building materials. For years, house builders have been requesting the elimination of that 11 per cent tax on building materials whose fall outs are heavily felt in the budget of all Canadian families, either in the monthly payment they have to make to pay for their house or in the rental payment they must make each month. The elimination of that tax would have been more beneficial and logical for the Canadian consumer than that proposed by the Minister of Finance for "candies" and bubble gum.
Secondly, the minister proposes an increase in the basic exemption on personal income; he also proposes to reduce personal income tax.
Let us say first of all that we do not understand how is it that between an income of $3,000 and another one of $6,000, the only difference in the tax reduction for the unmarried taxpayer earning that income will be a mere $2.
The same phenomenon recurs in the case of the salaried married man with two dependent children and whose annual income varies from $5,000 to $10,000. The wage-earner whose income is $5,000 will benefit from a $137 reduction a year, while another man earning $10,000 will have a reduction of $145 a year. How come the one earning $10,000 is entitled to a $145 reduction while the other who is getting $5,000 would only receive $137? The latter certainly needs a bigger cut than the one earning $10,000 a year.
The minister assures us in the budget that such measures will permit to salvage the family funds which are depleted by inflation and rising prices.
Looking at the statistics supplied by the minister himself on page 13 of the "Supplementary Information on the Budget" we notice first that, for instance, the married taxpayer with two dependent children under 16 and whose income is $6,000 a year will get a reduction in the federal and provincial tax of $139 for the year 1973. The amount of $139 annually corresponds to a $2.66 supplement a week in the taxpayer's pay envelope whose income
The Budget-Mr. Matte
is $6,000 and who, furthermore, has two dependent children under 16. A weekly supplement of $2.66 works out to 38 cents a day for four persons or, if you prefer, 91 cents a day per person. This 91 cents a day per person does not even buy a 10 cent chocolate bar from which the excise tax has been removed.
All this means, Mr. Speaker, that we should not be bowled over by the budgetary proposals of the Minister of Finance.
The married taxpayer with two 16-year-old children and an income of $6,000 will not even be able to buy a chocolate bar for 10 cents a day with the tax reduction the federal government has just granted him. This is for the birds.
Let us now look at this problem from another point of view, using the same example of a married taxpayer with two children under 16 and an annual income of $6,000.
After looking over the tables which the Minister of Finance himself supplied, we know this particular taxpayer will pay $139 less in 1973 for income tax. This means he will have $139 more in his pockets than before income tax reduction. On comparing with 1972, one wonders what will be the benefits for the taxpayer. According to Statistics Canada monthly publication no. 62-001 on consumer price movements, the consumer price index as regards food prices has risen by 13.6 per cent in 1972 and it stands at 150 for January 1973 compared with 136.4 in January 1972. As explained by Statistics Canada, this is a proportional increase of 10 per cent.
What is the equivalent of an annual or weekly increase of 10 per cent for food in a family budget for four people.
As usual, we are going to obtain an answer from the government itself in a bulletin released February 15 last by the Department of Agriculture under the title: "Tastes Dictate Grocery Bills". In that publication, the Department of Agriculture seems to insinuate that Canadians want to eat too well, hence the increase in the price of foods.
The Department of Agriculture shows three sample budgets for Canadian families.
The first one is a budget of misery which is pompously called moderate. It is set at $28.70 weekly.
The second budget which is highly recommended by the Department of Agriculture is an average budget for a family of four and which amounts to $47.76 weekly. Finally, there is the "generous" budget which amounts to $49.90 weekly.
For analysis purposes, let us study the intermediate weekly budget of $47.76 for an average family of four. I would compare this, Mr. Speaker, with the amount of $39 per person granted by the Quebec Department of Social Affairs, with the fact it is considered normal to spend $47.76 weekly.
If it is estimated that in theory the typical budget on January 1, 1973 would have amounted to $47.76 in practice it would have amounted to about $43, removing that 10 per cent because prices have increased by 10 per cent since January 1, 1972. This would amount to a weekly

February 21, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Matte
increase of $4.75 in the food budget of a family of four, over the year 1972, that is an annual increase of $247.
But what do they suggest to grant a family of four which draws an income of $6,000 a year? The Minister of Finance proposes to give it a tax reduction of $139. How can the minister explain that with $139 one can buy $247 worth of goods? This is a mathematical impossibility if one considers simply the case of the government concerning the moderate food budget introduced by the Minister of Agriculture.
What am I saying, Mr. Speaker? This average family of four whose annual income is $6,000 cannot even afford the low price food basket, the poor man's basket at $28.70 that the Minister of Agriculture suggests in the release that I referred to earlier.
Mr. Speaker, considering that the increase in the cost of living has been 10 per cent in the case of food over 1972, it can be said that today's market basket, costing $28.70, cost $25.83 in January 1972. We can say that basket now costs $2.87 more a week which for 1973 makes $149.24 more than in 1972. Now, the Minister of Finance has found no better compensation for that increase in the cost of food than a tax cut of $139. That family will therefore be $10.24 short for the purchase of a poor man's basket during the 52 weeks of 1973.
And that, of course, includes none of the other increases, rents, transportation, gasoline, medical care, leisure. Everything is increasing, Mr. Speaker, and we are all aware of that.
We have no congratulations to extend to the Minister of Finance for the minor tax cut he is offering the average Canadian taxpayer.
However, the minister did better when he announced an increase in old age security pensions. Of course, we know that these pensions will be increased from $82.88 to $100 a month beginning April 1, that is an increase of $17.22 per month. We believe that all Canadians who have reached pension age have the right to an equal pension sufficient to allow them a decent life. This pension must be high enough to enable them to benefit from Canada's wealth, from Canadian production and from all that the activity and genius of Canadian workers can make available to them.
This is why, we, of the Social Credit Party, are once more today proposing that the elderly person who retires should receive at least $200 per month whereas his or her spouse should receive at least $150 per month, no matter what his or her age.
We believe that the government has lost a magnificient opportunity to bring more happiness into numerous homes for the elderly in Canada by not allowing the spouse of the retired individual the right to receive this pension as soon as the breadwinner of the family or couple retires.
Nevertheless, we recognize that the government has taken a step in the right direction and we congratulate ourselves, of the Social Credit Party, for always having been at the vanguard of those who were asking for better conditions for the elderly and the retired whereas our

Liberal friends are only beginning to become aware of this. Not so long ago, Mr. Speaker, the government was simply refusing to increase the basic old age pension.
On May 4, 1970, during a vote on a motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg-North-Centre (Mr. Knowles) to increase the basic pension to $150 per month, the Minister of Finance and the right hon. Prime minister as well as the hon. member for Langelier voted against this motion while the Creditistes supported it.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), leader of our party, said at that time:
We support the objectives of the motion. For many years, we have called for a $150-a-month old age pension. We are calling for a similar pension for the blind and the disabled as a basic pension for all classes of society. We are in a position to do it because production in Canada can guarantee such a pension.
This is what the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada said on May 4, 1970 to support a motion to raise old age pensions, which was fought and rejected by the Liberal members who were then in this House.
Mr. Speaker, it can be said that only a fear of losing power, a fear of being defeated on the coming votes seems to guide this government who does not seem to have any social policy, let alone a family policy.
At least, this is what is suggested by Roger Bellefeuille, a journalist, in a study published in the Quebec Le Soleil on February 15 last.
On the subject of family allowances under the heading "The Cornerstone of a Social Policy", Mr. Bellefeuille writes:
Had the federal government officially advocated an "anti-family" policy, it could not have shown more reluctance, as has been the case since 1945, to offset more generously family expenses.
It may be argued that other so-called social measures, such as hospital insurance, medicare, the so-called free education, drug insurance for welfare recipients, help to alleviate the financial burden of families, the fact still remains that over the years, the steady increase in the cost of living has systematically eroded the purchasing power of families.
The cost of food products has increased by 52 per cent.
During that time, the federal government, with a disconcerting meanness, maintained family allowances at $6 a month for children up to 10 and $8 for those from 10 to 16.
It did not even deem it advisable to index them on the cost of living.
This was written last Thursday, a few days before the budget was brought down.
We, of the Social Credit party, find this attitude of the government shocking. We are shocked to see the present government pursue a policy likely to prove unfair to families, to reduce the birth rate, so that people, particularly in Quebec, become discouraged. And while forgetting its essential programs for family development and progress, the government seems inclined to talk even more of abortion. Such an attitude, Mr. Speaker, is somewhat shocking.
We feel that the government has missed the opportunity to give to all Canadians the economic security and social measures that they deserve.
We, of the Social Credit, have established a program; we put it to the people and, Mr. Speaker, in Quebec, where

our party is better organized than elsewhere, we have made more progress than all other parties.
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat in the House what we propose, so that the entire population will know what policy a Creditiste government will implement when it comes into power.
Mr. Speaker, the basis of our policy is to give a chance to all Canadians to achieve self-fulfilment. And since, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, the administration of all social measures comes de jure or de facto under provincial jurisdiction, we would obviously settle major problems by striking at their roots.
This is why we have included in our political platform, with regard to provincial rights, the following sentence: The Social Credit party of Canada will make available to all provinces the financial means they need in order to fully assume their constitutional responsibilities, without any interference from the federal government.
And further, we said: The Social Credit party of Canada believes that the present constitutional status quo, with which nobody is satisfied, must be left behind and the provinces must be given the power to be themselves, to develop and to fufil themselves, according to their needs and aspirations.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the dilemma facing the government and the Minister of Finance comes from what? It comes from a lack of co-ordination between the different levels of government.
This is why the Social Credit party of Canada said that the provincial governments should have their say in the development of monetary policies. The exclusive control of money and its extension, credit, through the federal government, the federal government's action on currency rates, on the money supply, on prices and inflation, have a direct influence on provincial finance and local economic development possibilities.
For these reasons, the provinces should participate in the development of those policies. In co-operation with the federal government, they should be able to turn their own credit into money in the same way as they are now able to borrow money on their own credit.
Some might say, Mr. Speaker, that the federal-provincial conferences are arranged to solve this problem, but everyone knows that those conferences have only one objective: to enable the ministers involved, in this case the Minister of Finance, to tell the provincial ministers, in a paternalistic way, that such is the Federal government's decision and that they can take it or leave it.
In the field of customs and trade, the provinces are now unable to protect their industries whereas the federal government can, through its power to negotiate or set customs tariffs-as mentioned in the budget speech- impose regulations on exports and imports, and thus considerably affect provincial economies.
We feel that negotiation of custom tariffs and settlement of extensive trade agreements should be done in consultation and with assent of provincial governments.
In respect of taxation, direct taxation was reserved for a very long time to the provinces because that was their only source of revenue. By its policies elaborated during
The Budget-Mr. Matte
the war, the central government tried to withdraw from the provinces that source of revenue; at the present time, the continuous presence of the central government in the field of direct taxation results in freezing and destroying all direct taxing powers of provinces.
The increasing needs of provinces in the field of education, social security and industrial expansion require that the provinces get back their direct taxing power.
Mr. Speaker, if we let the provinces administer as they want the matters under their own juridiction, probably there would be fewer constitutional conflicts, fewer fiscal conflicts and then it would be possible to implement the social security program we commended in the course of the last electoral campaign.
Mr. Speaker, we have repeated it many times: it is essential that some day-and that day should be much closer than we think-all Canadians should be given a guaranteed vital minimum income. Our country enjoys a fantastic amount of resources and it is unthinkable that the people should not take advantage of them.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion and further to the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), I move the following subamendment:
That the amendment be amended by striking out the period and by substituting the following:
"as well as the absence of measures designed to reduce the burden of the federal public debt and to stimulate the public financing of the provinces by interest-free loans from the Bank of Canada."

speakeroldname: Mr. Raynald Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the presentation of the budget last Monday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) seems to please most members, since it put together some realistic measures meant to improve economic prospects in 1973 for the individuals as well as for the community.
Mr. Speaker, we have endeavoured in 1972 to control inflation and unemployment, but I sincerely believe that the measures proposed in the last budget are really likely to make us reach our objectives, since they will promote the production rate and therefore employment. In addition, the budget has the great merit of enabling Canadians to benefit from higher incomes and thus increase their purchasing power. If a certain stability is maintained, especially as far as the American economy is concerned, 1973 should be a good year for the Canadian people on the whole.
But, obviously, everything is not perfect; I am sure that members of the opposition will agree with me and I should have liked to see certain questions included in this budget, for example, the question of shipyards.
I think we should tackle this problem as soon as possible because I consider that industry as essential from a defence and national economy standpoint. Our shipyards played an important role during the recent wars and one must recognize also that that industry now employs thousands of Canadians.
The last program called STAP allowed our yards to built 24 ships for foreign owners, in addition to acquiring valuable experience in the building of high-tonnage ships and developing new building methods. I think the government would be well advised to continue this program after March 31 and extend it to Canadian shipbuilders who could benefit from it, either by increasing or modernizing their present fleet. I hope the ministers concerned will take the necessary steps to ensure its continuance.
Another factor which affects the operation of our shipyards is the coastal traffic. The Darling report published in October 1970 made 15 recommendations to the government, the main purpose of which was to restrain coastal traffic in Canada to ships which displayed the Canadian flag. If they are accepted, the recommendations put forward ir: this report will have the following effect: they will give the Canadian government better control over its coastal traffic throughout Canada, enable it to derive a greater revenue from taxes on Canadian maritime transportation companies, give it a stronger authority in the Arctic waters, create more jobs for our sailors, and also encourage the operations in our shipyards thanks to the construction and repair of ships which will have to be built to meet these new needs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the interested departments, that is the Department of Transport and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, will implement these recommendations as soon as possible. Another thing which would have a substantial effect on the activities of our shipyards would be to set up a

Canadian merchant marine. This is something which has been lacking for many years in Canada, though our country is considered among the greatest countries in the world when it comes to foreign trade. Our economy would derive many benefits from it, given the ever increasing amount of goods and commodities like grain, oil, ore, coal, wood and many others which have to be moved outside Canada. It is difficult to admit that in this area, one can see almost no Canadian ships or ships displaying the Canadian flag. This is, I suggest, a matter of national pride which is quite important.
I would like as well to draw the attention of this House to the pension plan of the CN employees. We received a report by the Committee on Transport and Communications on this. The CN pension plan was considerably improved, but I feel that the most important matter has not been settled, that is the rate of pension payed to those who retire. Since they are employees of a Crown corporation, the CN employees now want to know why they are not treated exactly in the same way as the employees of other corporations under federal government jurisdiction. I think that the request is reasonable and even if there are certain adjustments to be made concerning the 1.5 per cent less that they pay on the part of their salary that they contribute according to the pension plans, there is no reason why these employees should not be treated the same as those who work in the civil service and why they should not benefit from the 2 per cent formula. This problem concerns 80,000 railroad employees and some of them come from my riding and I believe that if a solution is not found soon, the federal government would be justified in intervening. At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize the fact that I have been one of the main defenders of the railroad employees before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications because I believed and I still do that this claim on their part is fair and easily justified.
Another serious problem the farmers are faced with namely feed grain, has been overlooked in the budget. I would like the government to take steps regarding the supply of feed grain as soon as possible. This is a serious problem specially in Quebec and I think it would be possible to solve it, taking into account the volume and the price of grain in Quebec which are influenced by the federal government programs and more specially by those of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Quebec farmers request nothing but fair treatment. They do not want special privileges or better treatment than the western farmers. They do not want to deprive them of anything. All they want is equal treatment.
The Quebec Department of Agriculture and Colonisation, the Cooperative federee du Quebec and the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec has made nine recommendations to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and to the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, the major one being as follows:
1.	That feed grain transport assistance is an integral part of the feed grain marketing system in Canada.
2.	That the price of feed grains on the interprovincial market in Canada be based on the Fair Formula, provided that all grain producers in Canada are given equal treatment.

3.	That any procedure to minimize the cost of moving Prairie feed grains to consumer areas be encouraged.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, it would be high time for the federal government to make a decison, because seed time is only a few months away.
Another suggestion is related to housing. It seems to me it is about time for our government to consider the possibility of granting a tax deduction on the building of family type houses in order to encourage Canadians to become homeowners.
Since owners of public and commercial buildings are allowed to claim, each year, a certain devaluation of their property, it would seem logical that homeowners be entitled to the same privilege as well as to a tax deduction on the maintenance costs of such houses. As for the mortgage, it could also become deductible for income tax purposes. These are measures which would stimulate the construction industry, while achieving a purpose contemplated by this government, namely to allow a growing number of families to become owners of their own houses.
To conclude, I would like to raise an important matter, while it is of regional rather than national concern. For nearly 15 years, as chairman of the Lauzon Chamber of Commerce and member of a joint committee on the Levis-Quebec City direct link, I never stopped from advocating the establishment of that link, for the economic and regional development of our area, because this superstructure is essential. Recently, more specifically on February 20, the Hon. Bernard Pinard, Quebec Minister of Highways and Transport, released the report of experts who have proved that we were right in requesting a direct link. But one problem remains: the financing of the project, for it seems that a bridge would cost somewhere between $175 and $200 million. I therefore take this opportunity to ask what the federal government participation might be to that realization which cannot be postponed much longer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that one of the traditions of the budget debate, at least in the second round of speakers, is that members may range over a wide field in their comments; they may depart if they wish from strictly budgetary considerations and deal with matters relating to their ridings, as did the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) who spoke just before me.
This is also my wish, Mr. Speaker, but I propose to remain within the ambit of the budget debate by directing my attention to an area of endeavour which the government has consistently overlooked but one which, if properly treated, could be gratifyingly expansionary in a sector of the economy that is both labour intensive and is related to regional development, while taking into account Canadian tradition we have too long neglected.
I regret that in the course of the remarks by the hon. member for Levis the minister who is primarily concerned with them left the chamber because I, too, plan to direct my attention to that part of the amendment which regrets the absence of incentives to Canadians to increase participation in Canadian enterprise and development and to deal with the serious burden of unemployment
The Budget-Mr. Donald Munro
which afflicts our. country. I find it curious that the first speaker from the government benches should put his emphasis on programs which the government had decided in the past and in the present budget to overlook entirely. I suggest to him that he belongs to another side of the House.
My remarks today are derived from a multiplicity of sources. I speak of one of Canada's greatest traditions, an aspect of our native competence which is threatened by negligence and may disappear. I shall examine it in the context of our present economic plight. I shall also speak of the current unemployment situation in the country and of the growing need to exercise stronger controls over pollution in our waters and on our shorelines. If time permits, I will develop my second mix of thoughts. In doing so I will be drawing on a lengthy experience in serving Canada abroad and observing Canada from abroad.
It seems to me odd and distressing but true that, from time to time, we need to remind ourselves that Canada is a maritime nation. Too easily can we forget it; too often do we forget it, to our cost. I see the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) seems to have left. As I said, too often do we forget it, to our cost. We have been led to do so, I suggest, partly because of our continental fixation, our easy overland route north and south to markets, and partly because of Commonwealth preferences.
Two recent events, however, have shattered these illusions, namely, the restrictive trade policies introduced by President Nixon in August, 1971, and the entry of Britain into the European Common Market on January 1, 1973. The time has come, I suggest, to refocus on our maritime heritage.
In the deep sea navigable waters off the constituency of Esquimalt-Saanich, which include the Haro Straits and the Strait of Juan de Fuca-both of them running out to the international boundary-we have a special set of problems with which to deal. This is an international artery of commerce, and we want it that way. But in waters through which an international boundary runs, solutions of a particular kind are required. These solutions require the closest consultations between the national authorities who share the benefits of those waters as well as concerted action when action is needed. In a large measure, we do not have this co-ordinated approach at the present time, and it is high time we remedied that defect.
Before we can embark, however, on any bi-national program of co-ordination or undertake the international action that is required of us in our special circumstances on the west coast, we must consider a number of purely domestic concerns that deserve our attention, matters giving rise to problems that we must ourselves put right before we even think of trying to handle them in their international aspects. The first, of course, is the regulation and control of shipping of whatever registry plies our national waters.
As matters stand at present, Canada provides a variety of marine services: to cite only a few, these include lighthouse tendering, fisheries patrols, immigration controls, narcotics controls, dredging, icebreaking, happily not off my constituency, pilotage services, rescue, a sort of mini-

The Budget-Mr. Donald Munro
mum Coast Guard, and, in a very tentative sort of way, pollution control. All these services a maritime nation requires. In addition, a new duty has recently put in its appearance, the regulation and control of drilling rigs. These are appearing off the east coast, the west coast and in our northern waters. As well there are, of course, reconnaissance and search and rescue activities performed by our uniformed personnel. All these services are needed to an even greater degree than at present provided.
What is needed more is domestic co-ordination of all these services so that their provision may be supplied as, when and where required, and in the proper amount. There must be a means of overcoming overlapping jurisdictions and clashes of priorities which interfere with the provision of these services. According to the information reaching me, there is no single, co-ordinating authority in this complex area because civil and military authorities in Canada are each staking out their respective claims. Neither will let go and no superior authority, in this case a minister, is able or perhaps willing, to make a ruling and make it stick. Perhaps a statute is needed, Mr. Speaker. In the meantime, we are not providing all the services which our maritime status requires.
For example, we seem incapable of drafting and implementing regulations for the ordinary control of deep seagoing vessels of all kinds that carry all sorts of cargoes and enter our waters. We do not appear to keep records of the pattern of shipping entering our waters. This astonishes me. In the meantime, we provide many services that those ships themselves need, but provide them, perhaps, in an unco-ordinated manner. We do not require of those ships the standard of performance that we, a coastal nation with untold riches above and below the sea and on our shoreline, ought to insist on.
Let me cite examples. Such ships can enter our waters with semi-trained crews. They can enter our waters with only marginally seaworthy craft. They can travel on our waters without equipment that modern day developments ought to make mandatory. We need a full fledged coastguard to ensure that these and all other threats to our waters and shorelines are removed. In order to ensure that necessary action in this regard is taken in a coordinated fashion, I would be prepared to see our coastguard-I have already spoken about the mess of uncoordinated commands-placed under the ministry of transport for staffing and maintenance purposes but placed under the authority of the commander, maritime command for operations and tasking. This would provide satisfactory civilian careers, gratifying accomplishments and an effective service to Canada.
As of January, 1972, Canada could not boast of more than 86 vessels of all kinds operated by the Department of Transport to look after the needs of a coastline some 17,800 miles long. By contrast, the U.S. coastguard, with only 12,300 odd miles of coastline to protect, has almost 3,000 craft afloat. So, in one case 86 vessels look after almost 18,000 miles of coastline and in the other 3,000 vessels look after 12,000 odd miles of coastline. No wonder the United States coastguard is frequently called on to rescue seamen and fishermen in distress in Canadian waters. I feel ashamed that we have to go outside Canada

to obtain this kind of service. As a maritime nation, we must be prepared to carry our own weight at sea.
The establishment of a coastguard is one of my pleas, and a revived shipbuilding industry is another plea associated with it. Information reaching me causes distress, dismay and shame. One of our vessels now doing work on the west coast is due to be replaced. It is old and outmoded. According to the answer I received today, it is 20 years old and completely outmoded. The reply from the government side today indicates that the government is thinking about drawing up plans for a replacement. I have also heard that the present government is thinking of chartering out this work to a foreign vessel and foreign crew. This procedure, I understand, is already being followed either in the Great Lakes or in our Arctic. How, can we think of chartering foreign vessels to do work for Canadians in Canadian waters? Can anything be more outrageous in a maritime nation which is faced with high unemployment than going out of the country and obtaining both ships and crews that we can easily supply here? We have the capacity on both our coasts to build these vessels. On both our coasts, in our lakes and on our rivers, a Canadian coastguard such as I conceive it under a co-ordinated command could have as its supreme function regulating ships that ply our waters. They should be manned by Canadian crews and built in Canadian yards.
This brings me to another of my concerns. It is a concern of all Canadians, the pollution of Canadian waters and shorelines from accidents to ships at sea. We had such an accident on the west coast within the past month. We failed to get a full report from either the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) or the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) as to the full consequences of that accident. The pollution of Canadian waters and shorelines is becoming more susceptable to these accidents as our traffic increases and ships become larger, particularly tankers. Spills or sluicing bilges at sea or in Canadian waters is on the increase. These sorts of pollution must stop. They can be stopped only by effective policing. The most effective police for this purpose is a strong coast guard.
To bring these matters under control requires action on three different levels. We must be prepared to act in the international arena, the bi-national field and domestically we must get legislation on our statute books that will prevent Arrow disasters or Van Lean happenings as well as others that have occurred within recent memory. Above all, we must never permit a Torrey Canyon to happen on our shores or such accidents as happened just before Christmas in the Gulf of Oman, a collision and fire involving two midi-tankers. By midi-tankers, I refer to those ships of only 86,000 tons.
Canada and like-minded states should press for an international convention setting forth new seaworthiness criteria for ships and crews, criteria that will weed out hulks and thin out marginally qualified mariners, whether masters or crew. Failing that, we must at least have regulations, agreed upon with our neighbour, that will prevent inadequately inspected ships with semi-trained crews from sailing in our waters.
February 21, 1973
